performers: Carl Martin Öhmann, tenor; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Kerstin Thorborg sings the alto songs of the same concert)
intro: In the first song of Das Lied von der Erde, the wine is ready, and the singer calls for a song about death before anyone drinks. Carl Martin Öhmann sang it with Carl Schuricht in Amsterdam in 1939. The horns open the song, and the refrain rises a semitone each time it returns.

sections.label: A · horns and the golden cup
sections.mNote: The tenor sings against horns and flutter-tongued flutes.

sections.label: B · Strings, harps and solo violin
sections.mNote: Strings, harps and a solo violin play softly.

sections.label: R · First refrain, G minor
sections.mNote: The first refrain is in G minor.

sections.label: C · Second stanza: cellar and lute
sections.mNote: The opening fanfares return before the second stanza.

sections.label: R′ · Refrain in A♭ minor
sections.mNote: The same words, a semitone higher.

sections.label: Dev · Interlude for the orchestra
sections.mNote: An interlude leads to the earth’s returning spring.

sections.label: A′ · Opening fanfares; the ape on graves
sections.mNote: The opening fanfares surround a moonlit apparition on the graves.

sections.label: R″ · Toast in A major, final refrain
sections.mNote: A-major toast, then the last refrain in A minor

sections.label: Coda · Horns after the last “Tod”
sections.mNote: The first tempo returns for the orchestral close.

cues.title: Opening horn call
cues.text: The horns play a three-note call. Flutes flutter-tongue, muted trumpets rattle, and Öhmann sings high against the orchestra. The heading is Allegro pesante.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 3–5: Allegro pesante, muted trumpets and the tenor’s entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Li Bai’s source poem
cues.text: The song derives from Li Bai’s “Tale of Sorrowful Song”, which begins: “Sorrow comes; sorrow comes. Host has wine; pour not yet.” Bethge rendered this as “Schon winkt der Wein im goldnen Pokale, doch trinkt noch nicht”, and gave the song its refrain, “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod”.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Das Trinklied page, prints Li Bai’s poem in translation beside Bethge’s text, with the refrain, and Mahler’s alteration: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Das_Trinklied.htm

cues.title: “Wenn der Kummer naht”
cues.text: “Wenn der Kummer naht” — when sorrow draws near. The boast falls quiet. A solo violin and the harps accompany the lines about a garden in which joy and song wither, and Mahler marks the voice “düster, zart” — gloomy, tender.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 9–11, rehearsal figures 7–9. Hans Bethge’s text, adapted by Mahler; our translations.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First refrain, G minor
cues.text: “Dunkel ist das Leben, ist der Tod” (dark is life, dark is death). The tenor sings the refrain in G minor, accompanied by solo horn and harp arpeggios. At each later return the same sentence is set a semitone higher.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 11–12. Christian Utz, Musicologica Austriaca (2018), section 3, identifies the three refrain keys: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37. Bethge’s words; our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second stanza, Tempo I subito
cues.text: The horn call and the flutter-tongued flutes return at Tempo I subito. The next stanza is addressed to the host and his well-stocked cellar. The singer has brought a lute, and he holds a full cup to be worth more than all the kingdoms of the earth.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 13–21, orchestral return and Bethge’s second stanza as adapted by Mahler.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler’s resignation and losses, 1907
cues.text: In 1907 Mahler resigned from the Vienna Court Opera, “because I can no longer endure the rabble”, and on 21 June signed a contract with the Metropolitan Opera. Within weeks his elder daughter Maria died of scarlet fever and diphtheria. A doctor then found a defect in Mahler’s own heart.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s introduction for Universal Edition, March 2010, gives the resignation, the Metropolitan Opera contract of 21 June 1907, Maria’s death at Maiernigg and the valvular defect: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Second refrain, A♭ minor
cues.text: The second refrain is a semitone higher, in A♭ minor, and Öhmann sings the same words. Schuricht takes the refrains much more slowly than the drinking music around them.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 21–22. Utz, section 3 and Table 4, documents the refrain keys and Schuricht’s markedly slower refrain tempos: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Orchestral interlude
cues.text: The tenor rests for a long interlude. An oboe plays a solo, the flutes flutter-tongue and a muted trumpet plays above pizzicato strings. The harmony moves to A♭ major before the voice returns.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 23–26, rehearsal figures 25–30; Utz, Table 2, bars 203–260. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cylinders of Chinese music, 1908
cues.text: In August 1908 Paul Hammerschlag visited Mahler at Toblach and found him curious about China and Chinese music. Hammerschlag bought him phonograph cylinders of Chinese music recorded in China.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for Das Lied von der Erde, entry for August 1908: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-history/

cues.title: “Das Firmament blaut ewig”
cues.text: “Das Firmament blaut ewig” — the heavens are blue for ever. Bethge’s line sets the earth’s returning spring beside the short human life. After the strings play sempre ff, the tenor enters p ma appassionato.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 26, rehearsal figures 30–31: strings sempre ff and tenor p ma appassionato. Bethge’s words as set by Mahler; our translation. This is an existing cue for the passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Du aber, Mensch”, bars 298–299
cues.text: At bars 298–299 the tenor sings “Du aber, Mensch, wie lang lebst denn du?”, asking how long a man lives. Not a hundred years, he continues, to enjoy this rotten earth. A long intensification follows.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives prints the stanza: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Das_Trinklied.htm . Christian Utz places “Du aber Mensch” at bars 298–299, notes the indication Leidenschaftlich at bar 291 and describes the long intensification that follows, up to the ape scene at bars 353–368: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37 . Translation by the site.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening fanfares
cues.text: The opening fanfares return with glockenspiel, triangle and muted brass. The tenor sings of a shape crouching on the graves, an ape howling into the sweet scent of life.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 31–35, rehearsal figures 39–44. Utz, section 3, discusses the return of the opening music at bar 326: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The toast, Schuricht recording
cues.text: The singer now permits the wine. The toast opens in A major before the final dark refrain. Schuricht takes an extreme ritardando at bar 381 for the emptying of the cup, and Öhmann draws out “zu Grund” — to the bottom.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 35–37. Utz, section 3 and video example 5, analyses this recording’s extreme ritardando at bar 381: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37. Our translation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final refrain in A minor
cues.text: The final refrain is in A minor. On the last “Tod” (death), Mahler writes a diminished-seventh chord above the tonic bass. The horns and flutes then return to the opening tempo, and the orchestra ends the song on a short, hard chord.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 37–38, rehearsal 48 onwards. Utz, section 3, discusses the diminished seventh at bar 393 and the short final chord: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Into “Wenn der Kummer naht”
transitions.from: A · horns and the golden cup
transitions.to: B · Strings, harps and solo violin
transitions.how: After the held close of the first section, the music continues at Sempre l’istesso tempo, at the same pace. Strings and harps play softly around “Wenn der Kummer naht”, and a solo violin soon adds a phrase of its own. Mahler marks the tenor düster, zart.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition full score (1912), pp. 8–10, rehearsal figures 6–8.

transitions.title: Harp arpeggios and G minor refrain
transitions.from: B · Strings, harps and solo violin
transitions.how: The end of the garden stanza is marked Zurückhaltend. Ruhig. Harp arpeggios replace the repeated chords, and a solo horn accompanies the refrain in G minor. The tenor’s line is marked sehr getragen (very sustained).
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 11–12, rehearsal figures 10–11; refrain key in Utz, section 3. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: The horn call returns at Tempo I
transitions.to: C · Second stanza: cellar and lute
transitions.how: The held “Tod” meets a diminished-seventh chord over G at bar 90. Tempo I subito then brings back the horn call, with flutter-tongued flutes and glockenspiel. Open trumpets join the fanfare as it returns, and the strings play repeated notes.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 12–13, rehearsal 12. Utz identifies the chord over the tonic bass at bar 90: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: Second refrain a semitone higher
transitions.from: C · Second stanza: cellar and lute
transitions.how: The wine stanza ends on “Reiche dieser Erde”. A ritardando leads into a tempo, sehr ruhig, with harp arpeggios and plucked bass. The strings stay muted through the approach to the second refrain, which takes the first refrain’s G minor up to A♭ minor.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 21–22, rehearsal 23; refrain keys in Utz, section 3. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: A muted trumpet takes over
transitions.how: The held notes of the refrain run into an orchestral interlude in the region of A♭. An oboe plays above the winds as they die away. At a tempo, plucked strings and harp chords start again, followed by a muted trumpet and flutter-tongued flutes.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, p. 23, rehearsal 25; Utz, Table 2, orchestral interlude. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: Return of the opening fanfare
transitions.to: A′ · Opening fanfares; the ape on graves
transitions.how: The tenor finishes the line about earth’s rotten trinkets. A rising run in the woodwind leads back to the opening fanfare, scored with glockenspiel, triangle and muted trumpets. The low strings play pizzicato notes as the tenor begins the lines about the graves.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 31–32, rehearsal figures 39–40. Utz discusses the opening’s return at bar 326: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: Ape’s howl to the A-major toast
transitions.from: A′ · Opening fanfares; the ape on graves
transitions.to: R″ · Toast in A major, final refrain
transitions.how: The brass play the ape’s howl with bells raised, and cymbal and bass drum sound beneath them. A ritardando follows, and the toast moves into A major. Winds and horns hold sustained chords as the tenor tells the company to drink, and harp figures accompany the phrase as it slows.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 35–37, rehearsal figures 44–47; Utz, section 3, expanded final refrain. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

transitions.title: Diminished-seventh chord, then the horns
transitions.from: R″ · Toast in A major, final refrain
transitions.how: The last refrain moves to A minor. Its final “Tod” falls on a diminished-seventh chord over A. At Tempo I the horns play their opening call again, with the high woodwinds. The orchestra goes straight from the dissonance into its short final outburst.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 37–38, rehearsal 48; diminished seventh at bar 393 in Utz, section 3. https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, I. Das Trinklied vom Jammer der Erde, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 3–38: opening fanfares, three refrains, the ape scene and orchestral postlude.

timeline.note: The horns play a three-note call against flutter-tongued flutes and rapidly tongued muted trumpets.
The tenor enters mit voller Kraft against the full orchestra.
“Wenn der Kummer naht”: a quiet stanza scored for harps and solo violin.
The first refrain: sehr ruhig, a solo horn, harp arpeggios and held strings.
The opening tempo returns with flutter-tongued flutes, open trumpets and repeated string notes.
The tenor addresses the host above trombones and glockenspiel.
Harp patterns suggest the lute; woodwinds and trombones sustain beneath.
Two solo violins and a solo cello accompany the wine toast, with muted trumpets.
The second refrain, sehr ruhig, a semitone higher; the strings remove their mutes.
The orchestra alone: flutter-tongued flutes, a prominent oboe and marcato trumpet figures.
Violins and violas play sempre ff, using the G string, before the voice returns.
The tenor sings Das Firmament blaut ewig over soft winds and strings.
The tenor rests while winds and strings play the melody in F minor.
Harps and trilling woodwinds accompany the tenor’s question, “Du aber, Mensch”.
At Seht dort hinab, trills, brass and snapped strings surround the tenor’s line.
Muted trumpets, glockenspiel and triangle sound the howl.
At the climax the brass play with bells up, joined by cymbal and bass drum.
Jetzt nehmt den Wein: a quieter A-major toast with harps and horns.
Schuricht slows the emptying of the cup; the harps accompany the final refrain.
A fortissimo Tempo I postlude for the orchestra alone ends the song.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
